items.html_quote: 8-bit models barely change the photo; retrained ones leave blur; the paper's models peel the reflection off as its own layer.
items.paper_evidence: Sec. 5.2 says the published 8-bit DSRNet and Zhu "improve images modestly", while Zhang and CoRRN "distort the color" (e.g. Fig. 1). Supp. F.2 says Zhang's 8-bit model seems to have learned to remove blue-colored content. The 8-bit models therefore do not all merely leave the photo unchanged.
items.explanation: The blanket statement, repeated in the per-method captions (e.g. Zhang 8-bit "clean layer still looks much like the captured photo"), oversimplifies and partly contradicts the paper's description of color distortion and blue-content removal. The figure-level descriptions also cannot be verified from the paper text.

consistency.rationale: The page accurately conveys the problem (reflection removal for consumer RAW photos), the method (physically accurate RAW/XYZ simulation, a base model with an optional unaligned context photo, and a mask-based upsampler) and the key results. It reproduces the numbers I checked against Tables 1–3: the 1,241,091 training images, +70/+66 versus +48/+49/+28, the +40pp versus ≈20pp comparison, the All+G drop to +24, the upsampler PSNRs 47.77/43.29/42.24 and E2E 30.62/30.27, and the timings. It also candidly covers limitations: saturation and noise floor, texture overlap, rare scenes, saturated context photos, upsampler texture copying, and the lack of real-photo benchmarks. Omissions are minor: the lens-flare removal result, most data-collection and C5 white-balance details, the generalization-to-8-bit caveat (only briefly mentioned), and the overall framing of requirements. A few figure-content descriptions cannot be verified from the paper text.
missing_key_points: Lens flare removal as an unexpected generalization (Fig. S10)
Results on 8-bit photos via pseudo-inverted gamma, and the paper's statement that testing on 8-bit datasets is not meaningful
Training took 16 and 32 GPUs, with the base model's training details only in the deeper section
The paper's note that Photoshop edits used tone-mapped t and r because linear blending would be ideal

5.rationale: There is a kid-words box (ghost picture) and a projector analogy, but the page is mostly dense text, interactive charts and jargon. A pre-reader would grasp only the opening idea.

15.rationale: The "explain like I'm 8" boxes, the toy mixing lab and the glossary make the idea of adding light accessible. Sections with SSIM, XYZ and tone mapping are heavy, but terms are defined via tooltips.

25.rationale: The page is clear and accurate, with layered depth, tables, interactive toys clearly labeled as made-up, and the key numbers and caveats. A graduate can easily follow what was done and why it matters.

35.rationale: It gives a fast takeaway through the expert summary, stat cards and key-result callouts. Full tables and architecture details are available, and the page is honest about the small end-to-end gain and the simulated-only evaluation.

45.rationale: The practical impact (5 s preview, editable reflection layer) and trustworthiness caveats are explicit, including simulated test sets and no real benchmark. The page is long and technical in places.

55.rationale: The plain-language boxes, glossary and adjustable text size help. Terms such as SSIM, PSNR, XYZ and upsampler, and the many widgets, still demand effort for a reader unfamiliar with ML.

65.rationale: The page has a clear structure with TL;DR lines, a text-size control, a glossary and good contrast. The density, the interactive widgets and the dense numeric tables may overwhelm, and some jargon needs tooltips.
